name: Hesiod
credit: Roman bust sometimes identified as Hesiod (identification uncertain), Neues Museum, Berlin · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Hesiod was a Greek poet of Boeotia who lived around 700 BC, roughly contemporary with Homer. In the Theogony he says the Muses called him to song while he was tending sheep on Mount Helicon, and in the Works and Days he describes his father’s move from Aeolian Cyme to Ascra, and a dispute with his brother Perses over their inheritance.

He is credited with the Theogony, an account of the origins of the gods, and the Works and Days, a poem of moral and practical instruction for farmers. The Shield of Heracles has long been attributed to him but is thought by most scholars to be a later composition. Both works are presented here in the 1914 prose translation by Hugh G. Evelyn-White.
